meta.note: Where the stack physically is. Every site resolves to at least one station in the corpus, and every circle is drawn at true geographic scale — a ring of points each exactly `radiusKm` from the centre, walked around the compass, then projected. `radiusKm` is the extent of the site as it is publicly described: a science park boundary, an industrial district, a campus fence. It is not a claim about the buildings inside it.
meta.coordinates: Coordinates are for published corporate and public locations only, taken from company site pages, planning records and press reporting. Nothing here is more precise than the operator has itself made public, and `precision` says which kind of thing each coordinate is: `sited` — the operator publishes this location; `approx` — the right place, reconstructed from public reporting; `area` — a district or region, and the point is its centre.
meta.projection: Equirectangular. East–west distance is stretched by 1/cos(latitude), which is why the scale rings widen towards the poles. They are still true to the ground; the map is what is bending.

comparison.label: Milan
comparison.what: the administrative area of the Comune di Milano
comparison.note: Used for one claim only: that the circles this map draws around every leading-edge logic site, added up, enclose less ground than a single mid-sized city. The sum is computed from `radiusKm` at run time and the build fails if it ever exceeds this figure, so the sentence cannot go stale without someone noticing.

regimes.label: Writes the rules
regimes.note: A jurisdiction whose own export-control law reaches the leading-edge toolchain — in practice the United States, the Netherlands and Japan, whose three regimes together cover every machine capable of patterning at the leading edge.

regimes.label: Inside the perimeter
regimes.note: Has adopted equivalent controls, or hosts capacity that operates under them. Judgement, not a legal finding.

regimes.label: Restricted destination
regimes.note: A destination for which leading-edge tools require a licence that is, in practice, presumptively denied.

regimes.label: Outside the regime
regimes.note: Not meaningfully covered by the leading-edge control perimeter, which does not mean it is not a chokepoint.

sites.label: Spruce Pine

risk.note: Hurricane Helene flooded the district and cut rail and road access in September 2024; production restarted within a fortnight, and the fright did not.

sites.note: Two operations in one Appalachian district supply the overwhelming majority of the world's high-purity quartz, the material fused into the crucibles that every Czochralski silicon pull is grown inside. The crucible is consumed by the pull. There is no stockpile that lasts a year, and qualifying an alternative deposit takes several.

source.what: Helene damage at the Spruce Pine mines and the industry's exposure to them

sites.label: Mountain Pass
sites.note: The only rare-earth mine operating at scale in the United States, and for decades the world's largest before Chinese production displaced it. Digging the ore up was never the hard part; separating the elements from one another is, and that capability largely sits elsewhere.

sites.label: Bayan Obo
sites.note: The largest known rare-earth deposit on Earth, feeding the separation and metal plants at Baotou a hundred and fifty kilometres south. Light rare earths from here reach almost every motor, magnet and actuator in the stack — and almost every robot in stratum 24.

sites.label: Ganzhou
sites.note: Heavy rare-earth separation — dysprosium and terbium, the elements that keep a magnet magnetic when it gets hot. Separation, not mining, is the step that concentrates, and it concentrates here.

sites.label: Pingguo
sites.note: Gallium is not mined. It is scraped out of the liquor of alumina refining, which is why the country that refines the most aluminium also makes almost all the world's primary gallium — on the order of ninety-eight per cent. Export licensing since 2023, and a ban on shipments to the United States since December 2024, turned a by-product into an instrument.

source.what: Beyond Rare Earths — China's growing leverage over gallium supply chains

sites.label: Escondida

risk.note: In the driest desert on Earth; the mine now runs largely on desalinated seawater pumped 180 km inland and three kilometres uphill.

sites.note: The largest copper mine in the world. Copper is the least glamorous input in the entire stack and the one it uses most by mass — in the busbars of a rack, the windings of every transformer, and the interconnect wiring on the die itself.

sites.label: Salten
sites.note: Quartzite plus carbon plus an electric arc gives metallurgical-grade silicon, and the arc wants cheap clean power — which is why a step in the chain that begins in North Carolina passes through the Arctic Circle. Silicon smelting is one of the few places in this stack where the map is drawn by hydroelectricity.

sites.label: Odesa

risk.note: Production stopped in 2022. The industry rebuilt supply from Chinese and Korean capacity within about two years, which is unusually fast for this chain.

sites.note: Neon is a by-product of large-scale air separation, historically attached to Soviet-era steelworks. Two Ukrainian producers supplied something like half the world's semiconductor-grade neon before 2022 — the gas that fills the excimer lasers doing most of the patterning on every wafer.

sites.label: Ras Laffan
sites.note: Helium comes out of natural gas or it does not come at all, so the helium map is the LNG map. Ion implantation, leak testing and cryogenics all depend on a gas that only a handful of fields produce in quantity.

sites.label: Shihezi
sites.note: The polysilicon capital of the world — and almost none of it goes into a chip. Solar-grade polysilicon is six-nines pure and made here by the hundreds of thousands of tonnes; electronic-grade is eleven-nines, a market perhaps a hundredth the size, and made almost entirely by four companies elsewhere. The two are constantly confused, and the confusion inverts the risk.

source.what: China's share of global polysilicon capacity

sites.label: Burghausen
sites.note: One of the few places on Earth making polysilicon pure enough for a wafer — eleven nines, meaning one non-silicon atom in a hundred billion. The Siemens process that does it has barely changed in sixty years and remains ferociously energy-hungry.

sites.label: Hemlock
sites.note: The largest polysilicon producer outside China and the main Western source of the electronic-grade material. Four companies worldwide can reliably hit eleven nines; this is one of them.

sites.label: Shunan
sites.note: Electronic-grade polysilicon and a long tail of the specialty gases and precursors that go with it. Japan's chemical corridor is the least discussed concentration in the whole stack, and among the tightest.

sites.label: Kōriyama

risk.note: North-east Japan. The 2011 earthquake took resist and substrate capacity offline and the industry felt it for a year.

sites.note: Photoresist — the light-sensitive polymer that turns an optical image into a physical pattern. Japanese suppliers hold most of the market, and for EUV resist very nearly all of it. It is a material that cannot be stockpiled for long and cannot be substituted quickly.

sites.label: Imari
sites.note: Two Japanese companies make roughly half the world's silicon wafers between them, and the leading-edge share is higher still. A 300 mm prime wafer is the flattest mass-produced object there is, and the number of firms that can polish one to specification is in the low single digits.

sites.label: Freiberg
sites.note: Europe's wafer plant, in a town that has been mining and smelting since the twelfth century. It is a reminder that this industry did not choose its geography from a blank sheet — it settled where metallurgy already was.

sites.label: Gumi
sites.note: Korea's wafer supply, sitting a short drive from the memory fabs that consume it. Vertical proximity is the recurring pattern of this map: the heavier and more fragile the thing, the shorter the distance it travels.

sites.label: Veldhoven
sites.note: One campus in one Dutch town builds every extreme-ultraviolet lithography machine in existence. No leading-edge logic or DRAM is made anywhere on Earth without a machine assembled inside this fence. It is the single most concentrated point in the entire stack, and the reason Dutch export law is now a matter of global consequence.

sites.label: Oberkochen
sites.note: The mirrors. An EUV projection optic is polished until its worst deviation is a fraction of a nanometre — scaled to the width of Germany, a bump the height of a fingernail. One company can make them, in one town, and it has been in the optics business since 1846.

sites.label: San Diego
sites.note: The light source. Fifty thousand tin droplets a second, each hit twice by a carbon-dioxide laser to make a plasma that radiates at 13.5 nanometres. The source is a separate machine, from a separate town on a separate continent to the scanner it feeds.

sites.label: Wilton
sites.note: American-built modules go into every EUV scanner, and that fact is a legal instrument as much as an engineering one: US-origin content is what gives Washington a say over machines assembled in the Netherlands and sold to Asia. Export control follows the bill of materials.

sites.label: Santa Clara Valley
sites.note: Deposition, etch, planarisation and inspection — the four families of tool a wafer visits a thousand times — are designed within about forty kilometres of one another, in the valley the industry is named after. The wafers are made in Asia; the machines that make them are still argued about here.

source.what: Published headquarters — Santa Clara, Fremont and Milpitas

sites.label: Hsinchu Science Park

risk.note: Taiwan sits on the Philippine Sea plate boundary. A 1999 quake and a 2024 quake each cost the fabs wafers in process; the buildings are designed for it, the wafers are not.

sites.note: The park you could walk across in an hour. Fab 12 and the Baoshan Fab 20 sites next to it carry the leading edge and the research that becomes the next one. Every argument about concentration risk eventually reduces to this distance.

source.what: GIGAFAB facilities and Taiwan fab locations

sites.label: Southern Taiwan Science Park

risk.note: The 2021 drought put fabs on tankered water and reservoirs below a tenth of capacity. A leading-edge fab wants thousands of tonnes of ultra-pure water a day and cannot pause to wait for rain.

sites.note: Fab 18 — the eight-phase site that carries the 3 nm family at full volume. When people say a phone or an accelerator is made on 3 nm, in practice they are pointing at this rectangle.

source.what: TSMC fab expansion roadmap — the N3 and N2 ramp by site

sites.label: Central Taiwan Science Park
sites.note: Fab 15, and the 5 nm and 4 nm capacity that most of the current generation of accelerators was actually printed on. The leading edge moves; the fab that was the leading edge two years ago is where the volume still is.

sites.label: Kaohsiung
sites.note: Fab 22, ramping the 2 nm generation alongside Hsinchu — the first node built on gate-all-around transistors rather than fins. Two sites, four hundred kilometres apart, and both on the same island.

sites.label: Chiayi AP7
sites.note: The advanced-packaging site being built to be the largest in the world. Packaging, not wafer capacity, has been the thing rationing accelerators — an interposer is wider than a single exposure and has to be stitched, and very few lines anywhere can do it.

source.what: CoWoS supply-demand gap and capacity expansion through 2026

sites.label: Zhunan
sites.note: Where chip-on-wafer-on-substrate was industrialised, and where the hybrid-bonded 3D stacks are put together. Thirty kilometres from the fabs whose dies they join — which is not a coincidence, because a thinned die does not travel well.

sites.label: Nanzi
sites.note: The largest independent assembly and test house in the world. Most chips that are not accelerators are packaged by companies like this one, and the industry's quiet dependence on outsourced back-end capacity is roughly as concentrated as the front end.

sites.label: Pyeongtaek
sites.note: The largest semiconductor campus on Earth by floor area, and still building — P4 coming to full operation, P5 in main construction behind it. Logic and memory on one site, which is unusual, and a reminder that the memory maker and the foundry can be the same company.

source.what: Samsung accelerating P4 full operation and resuming P5 construction

sites.label: Icheon
sites.note: The home fab of the company that has led high-bandwidth memory through the whole AI build-out, and one of its three packaging hubs. HBM is the component that has actually been scarce, and this is where most of it is decided.

sites.label: Cheongju M15X
sites.note: A fab built specifically around high-bandwidth memory, pulled forward four months against its own schedule and starting HBM4-class DRAM in early 2026. When a twenty-trillion-won building gets moved up a quarter, the constraint it addresses is real.

source.what: M15X to produce DRAM in Cheongju

sites.label: West Lafayette
sites.note: An advanced-packaging plant for high-bandwidth memory, next to a university, in a state with no other semiconductor presence to speak of. It is the clearest single expression of the policy thesis that packaging — not wafers — is the capability worth relocating.

sites.label: Higashihiroshima
sites.note: The only leading-edge DRAM fab in Japan, and the site carrying the newest process node for an American memory company. Ownership and geography have not agreed with each other in this industry for a long time.

sites.label: Taichung and Taoyuan
sites.note: The largest share of America's DRAM champion's output is not made in America. It is made here, on an island the same company's customers describe as their principal concentration risk. Corporate nationality tells you almost nothing about where a chip is from.

sites.label: Boise
sites.note: American DRAM research, and the first new US memory fab in twenty years being built beside it. The gap between deciding to build domestic memory capacity and having any is measured in half-decades.

sites.label: Yokkaichi

risk.note: A 2019 power cut of thirteen minutes at this site scrapped enough wafers to move world NAND prices.

sites.note: One of the largest NAND sites in the world. Storage is the part of the stack nobody argues about until a training run needs to read a petabyte a second, at which point it is suddenly the whole conversation.

sites.label: Kikuyō
sites.note: A Taiwanese foundry building in Japan, next to a Sony image-sensor plant, funded substantially by the Japanese state. Not leading edge, and not meant to be — the point is automotive and sensor supply that does not have to cross a strait.

sites.label: Chitose
sites.note: A state-backed attempt to re-enter the leading edge from a standing start — a 2 nm pilot line running gate-all-around transistors on 300 mm wafers since April 2026, aiming at volume in 2027. Whether it works is the most interesting open question on this map.

source.what: IIM-1 Chitose, 2nm pilot line and FY2026 plan

sites.label: Leixlip
sites.note: The most advanced fab in Europe, and the only high-volume EUV site on the continent. Europe designs the lithography and polishes the optics; it prints comparatively little with them.

sites.label: Silicon Saxony
sites.note: Europe's densest semiconductor cluster, built on mature nodes for cars and industry rather than on the leading edge. It is a useful corrective: most chips in the world are not made at the leading edge, and most of the shortage of 2021 was here.

sites.label: Ocotillo

risk.note: The Sonoran desert. Fabs here recycle most of their water and the arithmetic still gets argued about locally every year.

sites.note: Where backside power delivery and the current American leading-edge process are being brought up. Whether the United States has a leading edge of its own in five years is mostly a question about this site.

sites.label: North Phoenix
sites.note: Taiwanese leading-edge capacity on American soil, and the most-watched construction project in the industry. It moves where wafers are printed. It does not move where the machines are built, where the resist comes from, or where the packaging is done.

sites.label: Hillsboro
sites.note: Process development, which is a different activity from manufacturing and a scarcer one. A node is invented in a place like this and then copied exactly — the industry's term is literally copy-smart — into fabs elsewhere.

sites.label: Malta
sites.note: A fab that deliberately stopped chasing the leading edge in 2018 and built a business on the nodes everything else needs. Most silicon in the world — power, analogue, radio, automotive — is made at geometries nobody writes headlines about.

sites.label: Zhangjiang
sites.note: China's most advanced foundry capacity, achieved without a single EUV scanner by pushing deep-ultraviolet multi-patterning far past its comfortable limit. It works. It costs yield, and it does not obviously scale another two nodes.

sites.label: Wuhan
sites.note: Chinese 3D NAND, entity-listed since 2022 and shipping competitive stack counts regardless. Memory turned out to be the part of the stack where domestic substitution moved fastest, because it needs fewer of the very hardest tools.

sites.label: Hefei
sites.note: Chinese DRAM, moving up the density ladder faster than most forecasts allowed for. It is not competing at HBM yet, and HBM is the part that matters for this stack — but the gap in commodity DRAM has closed considerably.

sites.label: Penang and Kulim
sites.note: Half a century of assembly and test, and now the place a large share of the industry's diversification is actually going. Back-end work moved here first because it was labour-intensive; it stayed because the skills compounded.

sites.label: Ōgaki
sites.note: ABF substrate — the laminate that carries an accelerator package and connects it to the board. It has been a bottleneck twice in a decade, it comes overwhelmingly from Japan and Taiwan, and almost nobody outside the industry has heard of it.

sites.label: Loudoun County

risk.note: Data centres took roughly a quarter of Virginia's electricity in 2025, and the queue for new connections is now the binding constraint on the county rather than land.

sites.note: The largest concentration of data-centre capacity on Earth — thousands of megawatts live, and about as much again planned — grown around the fibre routes laid in the 1990s. A large fraction of the world's internet traffic passes through this rectangle, and increasingly so does its inference.

source.what: Data-centre capacity and the Northern Virginia market

sites.label: Abilene
sites.note: A purpose-built AI campus on the Texas plains — several hundred megawatts running out of a design that scales to a gigawatt and beyond, sited for land, wind and an interconnection queue that moves. The site was chosen for its electricity, not its network.

source.what: OpenAI Stargate — where the US sites stand

sites.label: Memphis

risk.note: Brought up partly on on-site gas turbines while grid capacity was arranged, which drew local air-quality objections. Speed and permission are the same trade everywhere on this layer.

sites.note: A cluster stood up in months rather than years by treating the grid connection as optional and generating on site. It is the clearest demonstration that in 2026 the schedule constraint on AI compute is electrical, not electronic.

sites.label: Dublin

risk.note: New grid connections in the Dublin region have been effectively closed since 2022 — the first time a national grid operator publicly said no to this industry.

sites.note: The European precedent. Data centres reached roughly a fifth of national electricity consumption and the transmission operator stopped issuing connections. Every other market on this layer is watching what happens next here.

sites.label: New Albany
sites.note: Hyperscale campuses and a semiconductor build in the same county — a deliberate bet that co-locating the fab and the compute makes a region rather than two unrelated projects. It is early, and the fab has slipped more than the data centres have.

source.what: Central Ohio data-centre and semiconductor investment, 2022–2026

sites.label: The Taiwan Strait

risk.note: The circle drawn here is the strait at its narrowest — about 130 km across. It is drawn to scale because the scale is the entire point.

sites.note: The shortest distance between the world's leading-edge logic capacity and the state that claims it. No sentence about AI supply chains survives contact with this measurement: the substitute for Taiwan is not another island, it is a decade.

source.what: Minimum width of the Taiwan Strait, roughly 130 km
